fields.label: Selector
rows: The default, correctly pre-selected. Water, weather, ozone and UV — and it holds its grip cold, which is when a grommet is most likely to let go
Engine-bay panels — oil mist and weather together
Direct liquid oil. 🛑 Poor ozone resistance — not for an exposed exterior panel
Near a heat source. Tears more easily, which matters on a part pushed home by hand
Low-cost interior panels, no weather exposure
Best tear strength of the eight — a real argument where fitting damage is the problem, but it perishes outdoors
Hot oil-mist service. Cost rarely justified on a grommet
Aggressive chemical or very high temperature. 2–3× the cost
fields.note:
Live set: EPDM (SELECTED), NBR, Neoprene — three of eight, unranked, right one first.
Nothing is removed (client-instructed 2026-09-02): all eight shown and ranked, each with a reason.
The EPDM note is specific to this part. Rubber stiffens as it cools; a grommet retained only by grip is at its most vulnerable on a cold morning, and EPDM’s low-temperature behaviour is the reason it is the right default rather than merely a weatherproof one

fields.note: The production table in section 07 says first-pass yield is “On request” — the honest one is the table. The replacement puts this part’s acceptance criterion in the page’s most prominent slot

fields.label: Cards ×4
rows: Nothing holds it but the groove
No bolt, no clip, no adhesive. We size the groove to your panel gauge and set the push-out force you specify — light enough to seat by hand, firm enough that it never works loose.
A groove cut to bare-metal gauge is too tight once the panel is coated. Tell us the finished panel thickness and we mould the clearance in.
Open or closed, same tool family
Cable bore or solid blanking plug, moulded from the same groove geometry. One panel hole, two parts — useful when a variant deletes an option and the hole stays.
It has to grip on a cold morning
Rubber stiffens as it cools, and a grommet held only by grip is most likely to let go at −20 °C. EPDM is our default here for that reason, not just for weather.
fields.note:
Four cards, four cards — no count change and no new element.
Card 03 is a commercial argument disguised as a technical one. A vehicle or enclosure variant that deletes an option leaves the hole behind, and the blanking plug is a second part number off the same tooling — a supplier who says so is easier to buy from.
Card 02 is the detail nobody outside the trade knows, and it is exactly the kind of thing that causes a first-article rejection

sections.title: From compound to certification
sections.live: LIVE H2 → From Compound to Certification · six steps · “compression moulding” is right on this page

fields.label: Steps
rows: Material compounding — polymer blending, additive integration and batch QC in our in-house lab. Hardness is set here, and on a grommet held only by its own groove it is what determines the push-out force.
Mould design and CNC tool manufacture, in-house, held as a controlled record. The groove is cut to your finished panel gauge, coating included.
Compression moulding — [no change; correct on this part]
Post-cure and deflashing — flash removed from the bore and the groove. Flash in the groove is the difference between seated and nearly seated.
Quality inspection — groove dimension, bore diameter and push-out force checked against the drawing, plus hardness and batch sampling.
Export packaging — industrial packing with documentation. ISPM-15 treated pallets where timber packaging is used. Grommets are bagged loose so the retaining groove is not deformed in transit.
fields.note:
Six steps, six kept, and the process named is the process used — second sheet running.
Step 05 is where push-out force stops being a claim and becomes a procedure. Naming it as an inspection check, not just a specification, is what makes the rest of the page credible

notes: The process block must render from the part record — right here by luck, not by data.
Numbered steps are an <ol>.
